For us, a future-ready city is defined not only by technology, but by better governance, better data, stronger partnerships and more responsive public services. Our ambition is simple: to ensure that every community, regardless of size, location, is understood, included and served. That is what future-ready urban development means for the Bahamas— using innovation to strengthen institutions, using data to improve decision-making and placing people at the center of development. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Bahamas and all the delegations who participated. Those delegations who were not able to deliver their statements are kindly requested to submit their statements to estatements@un.org, and they will be posted on the United Nations Journal.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I warmly welcome all of you to the closing segment of the High-Level Meeting on the Midterm Review of the New Urban Agenda. I now give the floor to Ms. Ana Claudia Rosbach, Executive Director of UN-Habitat, to deliver some closing remarks.

Thank you, Excellency Vice President of the General Assembly. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. So over the past 2 days, we had member states, we had local and regional governments, entities of the United Nations, the civil society the private sector, the academia, many other partners coming together here in New York to take stock of the 10 years of the New Urban Agenda. And together we reflected on the progress that we have achieved, but also the challenges that remain, and most importantly, the actions that we really need to move forward, as it has been said in the previous panel, to keep the vision we embraced in Quito and make it a reality by 2036. I would like to express my most sincere appreciation to all the member states, all the partners, all the stakeholders that contributed to this process, the preparation of the national voluntary reports, all the interactive discussions that we had these 2 days, the process and the adoption of the political declaration. So your efforts, your collective spirit have really reaffirmed that the urban agenda the Sustainable Urbanization Agenda is actually one of the most important, relevant, powerful pathways for us to achieve sustainable development. I also wish to thank the President of the General Assembly for convening this very, very important meeting and all those who worked tirelessly to facilitate a successful successful outcome. The teams, the co-facilitators, we are here because the spirit of teamwork, collective work was there. So thank you, thank you very much. And this review has confirmed that the New Urban Agenda is today perhaps even more relevant than it was when it was adopted 10 years ago. The world is not the same world that we had back in 2016. It changed. So today, the speed and the impact of climate change is clearer and more intense. We see inequalities deepening, conflicts We went through a pandemic throughout this period, and when it comes to the basic, which is housing, affordability became a global crisis affecting all of us. So we have one message: the New Urban Agenda, its implementation, we have no time to lose. We really have to act. With urgency. And the choices that we make about how we address housing, how we address the land that we have, infrastructure, public space, governance, finance, all the indicators of SDG 11 will determine whether our cities become an engine of opportunity or resilience and peace, or places where inequalities and crises intensify. Over these 2 days, your messages have been very consistent. So you have recognized that we have progress. This is a reality. Many countries have actually adopted national urban policies. Housing became central and political agendas, and when it refers to the climate agenda, we realize that the urban issues are really firmly embedded across this discussion, but also the SDGs and the national development strategies. We improved our understanding of how important it is to address cities and housing right to get there with the global agendas. But also, you have been clear that progress has not kept pace with the scale of the challenges, as the DSG was just yesterday saying. Housing affordability has deteriorated, informality continues to grow, climate impacts are accelerating, and inequalities. Local governments are still constrained by the limitation of finance, capacity, autonomy, and on the other hand, there are more expectations from local governments. They are on the frontline, and this message came clearly across these days. We also understood that incremental change is not enough. We need to accelerate the pace for the second decade of the New Urban Agenda. We have to accelerate the pace and we have to do scale. So this high-level meeting has highlighted some priorities to guide us until 2036. I think the first priority, it was a common denominator throughout all these discussions is that we really need to place adequate housing at the center of sustainable development. We all understood that housing is much more than bricks. It's a social policy, but also economic policy, climate policy, health policy, and so on. And so really making sure that we all have access to adequate housing needs to be a priority for the next decade. The second message is that we really need to unlock finance for sustainable urbanization. Cities are generating the majority of global economic activities. They are responsible for 80% of the GDPs, but still the finance is not getting there. So we really need to work as one UN to make sure that member states are supported in leveraging domestic resources, local governments are resourced to increase their revenues, their local finance, but also working, as it has been said, with the private sector, leveraging private investments and the IFIs, the development resources and climate funding and the international resources that are out there. So there are resources, but we still need to channel the resources with the priority that cities, urban dwellers deserve. The third message is that we really need to strengthen multi-level governance and empower local and regional authorities. This was a central aspect of the New Urban Agenda, also of the work of UN-Habitat. We were just talking about the local toolkits. 2030, the coalition that brings 15 UN agencies. So localization of the SDGs for the implementation of the New Urban Agenda depends on strong institutions at the local level and resources at the local level. We cannot deliver the results by one level of government alone. The 4th message is that we must build cities that are resilient, that are inclusive, and that are future-ready. I really enjoyed the statement of the Mayor. We need to think ahead many, many years from now and have that in consideration. Finally, to conclude, this midterm review does not begin from scratch, these 2 days. We came from a 13th Urban Forum World Urban Forum in Baku, Azerbaijan, where we had strong outcomes, the Baku Call to Action by stakeholders, but also the summary of the first ministerial meeting on the New Urban Agenda. These have been pillars for this process and both reaffirmed the issues that we all discussed today, these days, and demonstrated a growing international consensus. Consensus around the need to accelerate implementation through stronger multilevel governance, increased investment, localization, innovation, and partnerships. We're all working together. Excellencies, together, all these outcomes complement the political declaration. They provide us with a roadmap for implementation. They help us to How the global commitments they they they they they take action on the ground, they reflect into practice. We have clear what's the responsibility before us. We don't we no longer have to define and agree on on challenges. We know how we have the solutions. We have the technology. We have enough pilots. We have enough commitments. So we have to really move. To systems, to investments, and from fragmentation to really integrated urban transformation. The ambition is there. We could see this these 2 days, and we are ready to support you, member states, local and regional governments, and work with all the stakeholders to get there. Partnerships are in place. Evidence is in place. So let's navigate after this strong political momentum here in New York, and let's make sure that by 2036, all cities, all communities can really contribute to a more inclusive, more resilient, more sustainable, more peaceful world. Thank you.

I thank the Executive Director of UN-Habitat. On behalf of the President of the General Assembly, I would like to thank all delegations for participating in this high-level meeting. Over 100 Member States inscribed to speak at the plenary segment, including 60 ministers, vice ministers, and high-level officials. About 300 stakeholders participated in the 4 multi-stakeholder panels, and the Political Declaration was adopted by Member States. The 2-day midterm review has given us a clearer picture of both our achievements and our shortcomings, and the Political Declaration has provided us with new opportunities— opportunities to build cities that are more resilient, more inclusive and more sustainable; opportunity to demonstrate that multilateralism can deliver practical results; and opportunity to be better together and ensure that no one is left behind. As the President of the General Assembly emphasized in her opening remarks, the only thing we are lacking is the will to scale up what works. I encourage all Member States to deliver the New Urban Agenda and the Political Declaration with concrete actions to every city, to everyone. The High-Level Meeting on the Midterm Review of the New Urban Agenda is now concluded. The meeting is adjourned.
